clinical.title: Design the first clinical study
clinical.question: What can this study teach us, in whom, and under what protections?
clinical.premise: A promising candidate needs a bounded human investigation with a clear question, interpretable measurements, and instructions for responding to risk.
clinical.inherited: Candidate pharmacology, exposure predictions, safety findings, and available human experience inform the study.
clinical.context: The first study under a US IND is not always the first human exposure.

nodes.label: Choose the question
nodes.question: What should we know after this study that we do not know now?
nodes.principle: Match the study's claim to the evidence its design can generate.
nodes.body: An early study may characterize safety, human exposure, or biological response. Establishing clinical benefit usually requires a different comparison, duration, and scale. Define the intended conclusion before choosing measurements.

items.label: Early learning
items.text: Characterize human exposure, tolerability, and biological response.

items.label: Definitive efficacy
items.text: Determine whether treatment produces a clinically meaningful benefit using an appropriate comparison.

items.label: Unsupported leap
items.text: A study may proceed, therefore its design will prove efficacy.

nodes.decision: State one primary learning objective and the conclusions this design will not establish.

nodes.label: Define the participants
nodes.question: Who can appropriately enter this investigation?
nodes.principle: Participant selection joins the biological question to the study's benefit-risk context.
nodes.body: Choose healthy volunteers or patients based on the intervention and question. Specify relevant disease features, prior treatment, and safety exclusions. A later population or longer exposure may need additional support.

items.label: Biological fit
items.text: Does this population let us investigate the intended drug action?

items.label: Clinical context
items.text: How do disease severity, existing treatments, and potential benefit affect acceptable risk?

items.label: Individual protection
items.text: Which findings or circumstances should exclude someone or require additional precautions?

nodes.decision: Define an eligible population and explain the scientific or safety reason for each important restriction.

nodes.label: Make results interpretable
nodes.question: Will the observations distinguish the drug's effect from other explanations?
nodes.principle: A measurement becomes useful when its timing and comparison support an interpretation.
nodes.body: Connect dose and sampling times to the expected exposure and response. Consider prior-treatment effects, baseline variation, controls, and assessment duration. A biomarker change may answer a pharmacology question without establishing patient benefit.

items.label: Observation
items.text: Measure exposure, biological response, or a clinical outcome at defined times.

items.label: Interpretation
items.text: Check whether the design separates treatment effects from competing explanations.

items.label: Next decision
items.text: Identify which result would change the next study or dose strategy.

nodes.decision: Retain measurements that answer the study question or change a safety or development decision.

nodes.label: Define action rules
nodes.question: What finding changes what happens next?
nodes.principle: Translate foreseeable risks into observations, review responsibilities, and actions.
nodes.body: Specify what to monitor and when, who reviews the findings, and when dosing or enrollment pauses. Distinguish an individual interruption from a cohort or study pause. Monitoring does not guarantee that every injury is preventable.

items.label: Before dosing
items.text: Confirm eligibility, baseline findings, and required precautions.

items.label: After dosing
items.text: Collect the observations needed to detect and interpret emerging risk.

items.label: Before proceeding
items.text: Apply prespecified review and action rules to continue, modify, or pause.

nodes.decision: Write an operating plan that investigators can implement consistently, including the information required before escalation.

cases.name: Oteseconazole
cases.stage: Initial IND, 2011; retrospective NDA history also describes later Phase 2a advice.
cases.context: An oral antifungal entered an initial randomized, blinded, placebo-controlled single-dose study in healthy adults.
cases.known: The protocol specified safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics as its early human questions.
cases.supports: The design could characterize single-dose human exposure and tolerability within the studied conditions.
cases.uncertain: It did not establish clinical benefit. The public history does not reproduce the complete original protocol.
cases.decision: FDA identified no initial clinical-hold issues. Later, it called a Phase 2a study exploratory and requested stronger statistical testing for definitive conclusions.
cases.lesson: Choose the question first; an early learning study and a definitive efficacy study need different support.

cases.name: Levacetylleucine
cases.stage: Pre-IND, 2018, and initial IND, 2019; retrospective NDA history. Not a conventional first-ever-human study of an entirely unfamiliar intervention.
cases.context: An open-label study in Niemann–Pick disease type C followed earlier experience with racemic acetylleucine.
cases.known: FDA considered an open-label design potentially useful for proof of concept, but inadequate for interpretable marketing-application efficacy evidence.
cases.supports: A limited exploratory investigation could provide short-term safety information and inform further study design.
cases.uncertain: Without an adequate comparison, observed changes could not reliably establish treatment benefit. Several details in the public history are redacted.
cases.decision: The sponsor acknowledged the exploratory purpose, removed an extension, and limited the study to six weeks. FDA issued a may-proceed letter and recommended further design discussion.
cases.lesson: Permission to conduct a study does not establish that its design can prove efficacy.

exercise.title: Define what the study can conclude
exercise.context: A team proposes a short, uncontrolled study in patients. It will measure safety, drug exposure, and a disease biomarker. Prior therapy may still influence that biomarker. The supporting package addresses the proposed exposure and known risks.
exercise.claim: If the study can proceed and the biomarker improves, we will have established clinical benefit.
exercise.prompt: Which revision best connects the design to an appropriate conclusion?

options.label: Keep the claim because the package supports exposing participants.
options.feedback: Support for the proposed exposure does not establish that the study can distinguish treatment benefit from other explanations.

options.label: Define the study as exploratory, address prior-treatment effects, and plan the comparison needed to test benefit.
options.feedback: This preserves useful early learning while matching the claim to what the design can establish. The safety plan and the efficacy interpretation remain separate judgments.

options.label: Add more biomarkers and keep the same efficacy claim.
options.feedback: More measurements do not remove confounding or provide a missing comparison. Select observations that resolve the question rather than multiplying endpoints.

result.claim: The study can support exploratory human learning within its stated limits.
result.support: Safety, exposure, and biomarker observations answer defined early questions.
result.uncertainty: Prior therapy and the missing comparison limit attribution of benefit.
result.next: Revise the interpretation plan and define the later study needed to test clinical benefit.

boundary.required: The IND protocol must describe objectives, participant selection, dose determination, exposure duration, observations, and procedures to minimize risk, with safety-critical details appropriate to the phase.
boundary.recommended: FDA guidance and program-specific advice can inform study design. A historical protocol is not a universal template.
boundary.judgment: The team chooses the learning objective, population, measurements, and action rules, and must explain how they fit the evidence and remaining uncertainty.

handoff.label: Justify the starting dose and escalation
handoff.text: Use the defined population and study conditions to justify the first dose and the evidence needed before going higher.

clinical-dose.title: Justify the starting dose and escalation
clinical-dose.question: Why begin at this dose, and what evidence would justify the next step?
clinical-dose.premise: The first dose is a prediction with uncertainty. A reassuring starting margin does not justify every later dose or schedule.
clinical-dose.inherited: Relevant pharmacology, toxicology, exposure measurements, formulation information, and any prior human experience support the dosing rationale.
clinical-dose.context: Healthy volunteers, advanced cancer, local administration, and first dosing in children require different considerations.

nodes.label: Choose the framework
nodes.question: Which dose-selection approach fits this population and intervention?
nodes.principle: Select the clinical context before selecting a calculation.
nodes.body: Healthy-volunteer MRSD guidance has a defined scope; it does not determine escalation limits. Advanced-cancer and locally administered products require their own context. Prior human experience may inform a new population without eliminating its uncertainties.

items.label: Healthy volunteers
items.text: Consider the scoped MRSD framework and pharmacological activity.

items.label: Advanced cancer
items.text: Consider disease severity, available therapy, and relevant oncology guidance.

items.label: New population
items.text: Ask what prior human experience can support and what does not transfer.

nodes.decision: State the selected framework and explain why it applies to this study.

nodes.label: Identify the anchor
nodes.question: Which biological findings meaningfully constrain human dosing?
nodes.principle: A tested dose, observed effect, and relevant exposure must be interpreted together.
nodes.body: Identify the relevant species or human system, observed toxicity or pharmacological effect, and exposure conditions. A NOAEL describes the study performed; absent findings do not establish that all higher exposures are harmless.

items.label: Observed finding
items.text: What happened at the doses and durations actually tested?

items.label: Human relevance
items.text: Does the system represent the drug's human pharmacology and possible hazards?

items.label: Evidence limit
items.text: Which effects, exposures, or populations remain uncharacterized?

nodes.decision: Identify the reference finding, its exposure basis, and the uncertainty it leaves.

nodes.label: Predict the start
nodes.question: How does the evidence support the proposed first human exposure?
nodes.principle: A numerical dose proposal needs explicit assumptions about human exposure and response.
nodes.body: Use a justified translation method and account for uncertainty. Compare the predicted exposure with relevant safety and pharmacology findings. An animal-equivalent dose or model output is a prediction, not a measured human result.

items.label: Measured evidence
items.text: Relevant experimental exposure and biological effects.

items.label: Translation
items.text: Scaling or modeling, species differences, and justified uncertainty allowances.

items.label: Proposed start
items.text: A bounded first dose with an expected exposure range to test.

nodes.decision: Document the starting-dose rationale and identify which human observations will test its assumptions.

nodes.label: Constrain and update
nodes.question: What must be learned before increasing dose or repeating treatment?
nodes.principle: Starting dose, escalation, and the eventual regimen are separate decisions.
nodes.body: Assess the upper-dose and repeat-dose support separately. Use observed human PK, biological response, and safety to update the plan. Specify review conditions and actions when exposure or effects differ from predictions.

items.label: Begin within bounds
items.text: Use the justified starting dose and planned precautions.

items.label: Measure and compare
items.text: Compare observed exposure and effects with the prediction.

items.label: Decide the next step
items.text: Proceed, modify, or pause using the evidence and specified rules.

nodes.decision: Define what supports going higher, what remains unsupported, and what would change the dosing plan.

cases.name: Ivacaftor
cases.kicker: A start is not a ceiling
cases.stage: Original initial IND review, reproduced in the 2012 NDA package.
cases.context: Short repeat-dose animal studies supported a proposed first dose, but did not identify target organs to guide monitoring at higher exposure.
cases.known: The reviewer reported large margins at the proposed 25 mg start, but only about twofold at the proposed 800 mg maximum. Target-organ toxicity remained incompletely characterized.
cases.supports: The evidence supported a limited initial clinical plan, with separate consideration of the upper dose.
cases.uncertain: No target organ was identified in the short repeat-dose studies. Absence of findings did not characterize the potential toxicity at higher exposures.
cases.decision: The reviewer accepted a modified 500 mg maximum and recommended higher-dose nonclinical work to characterize potential target organs. These are historical study-specific numbers.
cases.lesson: A large starting margin does not establish an unrestricted escalation path.

cases.name: Risdiplam
cases.stage: First infant dosing during clinical development, after adult exposure; described retrospectively in the NDA review. Not first-ever-human dosing.
cases.context: In infantile-onset spinal muscular atrophy, the team needed to begin dosing a vulnerable population and learn how measured exposure compared with predictions.
cases.known: A conservative physiologically based PK prediction and an additional safety factor informed the first infant's single dose. Human PK was then measured.
cases.supports: The observed single-dose PK informed subsequent repeated dosing and exposure targets linked to expected biological response.
cases.uncertain: The first observation did not establish long-term safety or clinical benefit. The public account does not reproduce an original FDA approval of the dose calculation.
cases.decision: After evaluating single-dose PK and tolerability, the team selected repeat dosing. Internal and independent committees reviewed safety, PK, and PD for further dose decisions.
cases.lesson: Use human observations to test a dose prediction before extending the regimen.

sources.label: First infant dose and reassessment · PDF73–74

exercise.title: Separate the starting point from the path
exercise.context: A candidate's short repeat-dose studies found no adverse effects at the highest doses tested. The proposed human starting dose has a reassuring margin. The planned escalation reaches much higher predicted exposures, where the toxicity profile remains uncertain.
exercise.claim: The large starting-dose margin supports the entire escalation plan.
exercise.prompt: Which team decision best reflects the evidence?

options.label: Proceed through every planned dose because the animal studies were clean.
options.feedback: The studies characterize tested conditions. They do not establish that higher exposure is harmless or identify what would need monitoring there.

options.label: Reject the candidate because no target-organ toxicity was found.
options.feedback: An incompletely characterized hazard does not itself require abandoning the molecule. A narrower plan and targeted evidence may address the uncertainty.

options.label: Assess upper-dose support separately, bound escalation, and define the human observations and additional evidence needed to proceed.
options.feedback: The starting point can be supported while later steps remain uncertain. Define the permitted path from the actual evidence and revise it as human findings accumulate.

result.claim: The evidence may support a bounded initial study, not every planned escalation.
result.support: The proposed starting exposure has a justified relationship to the available findings.
result.uncertainty: Higher-exposure hazards and appropriate monitoring remain incompletely characterized.
result.next: Set a supported escalation boundary and specify the evidence needed before extending it.

boundary.required: The protocol must describe dose determination, planned maximum dosage, exposure duration, and procedures to monitor effects and minimize participant risk.
boundary.recommended: FDA's adult healthy-volunteer MRSD framework primarily addresses systemic starting doses. It does not determine escalation limits or apply unchanged to every patient population.
boundary.judgment: The team selects relevant evidence, translation methods, uncertainty allowances, and escalation conditions appropriate to the intervention and study.

handoff.label: Ask a useful pre-IND question
handoff.text: Bring the study, dosing proposal, supporting evidence, and unresolved question together for a focused discussion.
